findings.title: Band choice is a free pick from a list with the answer shown live, so trying all five keys solves every delivery without any understanding
findings.problem: The room's main idea is which wavelength gets through which material. The player meets that idea only as five buttons (keys 1–5, station.ts:221 and :366). Every press updates the result before anything is committed. The link screen turns green and reads CLEAR LINK (station.ts:338). The side panel switches 'Path' from 'blocked: brick wall' to 'clear' and shows the margin in dB (station.ts:423-427). The map draws the beam up to its red X (station.ts:310-313). None of this costs a mistake, because only SEND counts (station.ts:231-232). The prompt even says what to do next: 'Aim, or another band' / '1–5 Another band' (station.ts:442). Job 1 took one press: Visible showed BLOCKED (shot 03), RADIO showed 11 dB CLEAR LINK (shot 05). Job 3 is the same: cycle until it goes green (shots 20, 22, 24). Nobody has to predict anything, because the screen answers before the player commits. The sweep (tools/spectrum-teach/sweep.mjs output) shows each job has one obvious green band, so cycling always finds it in at most 5 presses at zero cost. This breaks 'the mechanic is the concept' and 'predict before you test'. A player can earn three Elegant deliveries and leave believing 'press buttons until it goes green'. The mirror aiming is a real physical act and works well. The wave-versus-material idea, the core of the room, has no act at all.
findings.fix:
Commit first, reveal after:
(1) Before SEND, the map shows the band's planned straight ray as a thin dashed line, without the stop X. The link screen shows only the inputs (band, λ, power, and the materials the ray will cross, as icons). In updatePanel (station.ts:426-427), hide the 'Path' and 'Link margin' rows until a pulse has run for the current band and setup.
(2) SEND fires the pulse (firePulse already exists, station.ts:241). The result appears where the pulse stops or arrives.
(3) Turn the wall chart (room.ts:134-140) into a lab notebook that starts empty. Each cell fills in when the player first sees that band meet that material. The player learns the table by testing it, not by reading it.
(4) Keep failed sends cheap (they are). A 'test send' could cost one energy unit (POWER_COST) so cycling has a small cost and brute force can't earn Elegant (DR-38).
(5) Change the prompt at station.ts:442 to 'Enter Send' whatever the setup, so it no longer says 'another band'.
findings.verify: New spec in tests/station-spectrum.spec.ts: at the desk, cycle bands 1–5 without SEND. `.station-panel` must not contain 'dB' and the link screen key must not read CLEAR LINK. After SEND the reading appears. Retake spectrum-teach-03/05 and check that no margin is visible before the send.
findings.verify_reason: I reproduced this myself. With the pod on the store pad I pressed bands at the desk and never sent. Radio showed 'CLEAR LINK 11.0 dB' with 'Path clear' and the prompt 'Enter Send' (verify-spectrum-teach-11-desk-cycle-radio.jpg). Visible, thermal and near IR showed 'blocked: brick wall'. Microwave showed 7.0 dB. snap() gave mistakes 0 and spent 0 after all five presses. In the code, the band act sets the band and detector (station.ts:221), and updatePanel, drawLink and drawMap redraw every frame from read() (station.ts:404, :423-427, :338, :310-313). One correction to the claim: job 2 can't be solved by cycling alone. Every band is 'Metal shutter' without a mirror (my logic sweep), so the player must place and aim a mirror first. After that, cycling vis/NIR shows 5.8 vs 10.8 dB live. Jobs 1 and 3 are solved by cycling at zero cost. This breaks DR-31 (results before testing) and DR-38.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-spectrum-teach/logic-check.ts (lab: every band and power 'Metal shutter' without a mirror)
findings.fix_correction: Point (4) is already partly true. A failed SEND already charges energy (station.ts:231 adds the cost to spent before the tier check) and counts as a mistake (No failed send bonus). What costs nothing is the live preview, so fix that instead of adding a cost to sends. Hide the 'Path' and 'Link margin' rows and the CLEAR LINK / TOO WEAK / BLOCKED status until a pulse has run for the current band and setup. Keep the aimed geometry (traceBeam reflections) drawn, because aiming is the room's one physical act and needs live feedback. Draw it without material stop marks. Pointer (5) is also right: drop 'another band' from station.ts:442.

findings.title: The 'copper-mesh cage' quiet room has an open 1.6 m doorway and mesh on only two sides, yet the game says the cage keeps Wi‑Fi out
findings.problem: Job 3 teaches that a mesh cage reflects radio and microwaves (LOSS.mesh radio/micro = Infinity, logic.ts:75; message logic.ts:258). In the model, QUIET has mesh walls only on its side (x0) and its front up to the door. The doorway from x 9.4 to 11 is open (logic.ts:99, :112-113, room.ts:105). The other two sides are the hall's plain outer walls. Pip walks in and out through that gap (shot 32). The link model traces one straight ray from the tower, and that ray happens to cross the mesh, so microwave counts as 'blocked'. A real 2.4 GHz wave (λ 12.5 cm) passes a 1.6 m opening (about 13 λ) almost unchanged. Shielding guidance says doors and seams dominate leakage: an unbonded closed door is still a big opening, let alone an open one. The game shows a screened room with its door wide open and calls it screened. The learner takes away a wrong rule: a few mesh panels block signals. They also miss the real one: a cage must be closed all round. The lesson is truthful only along the drawn ray.
findings.fix:
Make the cage closed and make closing it a physical act.
(a) In room.ts, add a mesh door leaf on the QUIET door segment (9.4–11, z 1.5). It swings shut on a spring after Pip passes, like the lobby doors. Line the two hall-shell faces inside the quiet room with the same mesh texture.
(b) In logic.ts, add a 'quiet-door' wall whose material is 'mesh' when shut and an opening when open. Add a `cageShut` field to Setup.
(c) When the door is open, radio and microwave reach the pod through the doorway (charge the extra spreading only). That gives a truthful chaos and alternate route: prop the cage door open and Wi‑Fi gets in, but the sleepy reader wakes and complains, so the job asks for the door shut.
(d) Change whyBlocked('mesh') to: 'The cage is closed all round with fine copper mesh: microwaves reflect off it. Light slips between the wires.'
findings.verify: Unit test in src/stations/spectrum/logic.test.ts: with cageShut=false, micro at 10 mW reaches the quiet pad. With cageShut=true it is blocked by mesh. Retake spectrum-teach-32 and check that a door leaf closes the opening.
findings.verify_reason: walls() defines only 'quiet-side' (x=5.5) and 'quiet-front' (z=1.5, x 5.5 to 9.4) as mesh (logic.ts:112-113). QUIET.door [9.4,11] has no wall (logic.ts:99). QUIET.x1=11 and z1=8 equal HALL {x:11,z:8} (logic.ts:195), so the other two faces are the hall shell. room.ts:105 builds only those two meshWalls. Shot spectrum-teach-32 shows Pip standing in the open gap at the end of the mesh run, with the hall's outer rail beyond. The link model counts a single crossing of the mesh panel at (5.5, 4.0), which my geometry check confirms. The physics claim about a 1.6 m opening at λ = 12.5 cm is correct. The doorway faces away from the tower, so in reality the leak would come in via hall reflections, which this model leaves out (logic.ts:24-26). That doesn't make the drawn 'screened' cage any less wrong.

findings.title: The cage mesh drawn on screen has about 6 cm holes, half of Wi‑Fi's 12.5 cm wave, so it would barely shield; the text says the holes are 'far smaller than the wavelength'
findings.problem: meshTex (room.ts:26) draws 8 cells per 128 px tile, and each tile is repeated over 0.5 m (room.ts:99, `t.repeat.set(len/.5,mh/.5)`). Each hole is therefore 0.5/8 = 6.25 cm, which is clearly visible next to Pip (shots 30, 34). The failure message says 'its holes are far smaller than the microwave wavelength' (logic.ts:258). The bench shows λ 125 mm for microwave (shot 21). A curious player who compares the two sees holes at λ/2. The common rule is openings below λ/10, about 1.25 cm here. The usual estimate SE ≈ 20·log10(λ/2d) gives about 0 dB at d = λ/2, so a mesh this coarse is nearly transparent to 2.4 GHz. The picture and the sentence contradict each other, and the picture implies the wrong threshold.
findings.fix: Change meshTex to a fine weave: 32 lines per 128 px over a 0.25 m repeat, which gives about 8 mm holes, below λ/10. Keep the copper posts and the top and bottom rails as the readable structure, so the fine mesh doesn't shimmer as moiré at the game camera. Alternatively keep the coarse texture at alpha 0.4 and lay a fine-weave overlay on top. Add a small mounted plaque on a copper post: 'mesh holes 8 mm · Wi‑Fi wave 125 mm'. That puts the size comparison in the world.
findings.verify: Zoom-9 crop of the cage (retake spectrum-teach-30). Count about 30 holes per 0.25 m, and confirm the hole size reads clearly smaller than the 12.5 cm λ ribbon when microwave is selected.
findings.verify_reason: meshTex draws lines every 16 px on a 128 px canvas, so 8 cells (room.ts:26). meshWall repeats the tile every 0.5 m (room.ts:99, t.repeat.set(len/.5, mh/.5)), so holes are 6.25 cm. Shot spectrum-teach-30 shows large, clearly countable cells next to Pip. Shot 21 shows λ 125 mm and the 'holes are far smaller than the microwave wavelength' toast together. A hole of λ/2 is not 'far smaller'. This breaks DR-34 (wording physically right).
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/spectrum-teach-21-job3-micro-fail.jpg (viewed: λ 125 mm next to the 'far smaller' toast)
findings.fix_correction: At 32 lines per 128 px, keep lineWidth 3 and the canvas is mostly copper. Drop lineWidth to about 1 and let mipmaps / anisotropy handle it, or use the 'coarse frame + fine overlay at low alpha' alternative. That avoids moiré at the 9 to 38 m camera distances.

findings.title: Radio is 'stopped by the metal shutter' at the lab, although the lab's side wall is brick (which job 1 just taught radio passes) and its door is open; the broadcast rings promise spreading that the direct-ray model doesn't do
findings.problem: Job 1 teaches 'the 3 m radio wave passes brick' (shots 05-06). In job 2, LAB's left wall `lab-side` is brick (logic.ts:107). LAB.door [9.4,11] is an open 1.6 m doorway (logic.ts:98), and Pip carries the pod through it (shot 33). Radio and microwave are drawn as broadcasts, with expanding rings in the hall (station.ts:164-165, :392) and on the map (station.ts:311). They are priced along a single straight line, TX→pad (logic.ts:24-26, :187). That line hits the metal front, so the verdict is 'Metal shutter: Metal reflects radio: the shutter stops it' at every power and hatch setting (sweep output, shots 11 and 41). In reality an FM signal fills the hall and reaches the lab through the brick side wall (−4 dB in the game's own table) and the open door. A learner who correctly generalises job 1 ('radio spreads out and gets through brick') is told they are wrong. The broadcast rings drawn on screen are contradicted by the result. The room's own lesson teaches 'radio travels in a straight line like a beam', which is the opposite of the visual.
findings.fix:
Make the lab a real metal box and the broadcast a real broadcast.
(1) logic.ts walls(): change `lab-side` to ['metal','brick'] (a metal-clad clean lab) and add a closed metal lab door on LAB.door. In room.ts, add the door leaf with a spring so Pip can still enter, and add slat cladding on the side wall.
(2) For non-beam bands, price the best of several candidate paths instead of only the direct ray: the direct ray, and TX→each opening→pad (openings: the hatch when open, the cage door when open). Radio through the 60 cm hatch is then blocked by the λ/2 rule. Microwave through the open hatch gets its 8 dB.
(3) On the map, draw broadcasts as rings only, with no straight ray (station.ts:312 draws a dashed ray). Mark each opening it leaks through.
findings.verify: Unit tests in src/stations/spectrum/logic.test.ts: lab + radio is blocked with mat 'hatch' when the hatch is open (not 'metal'). Lab + micro at 10 mW with the hatch open is reliable through the hatch. Retake spectrum-teach-11 and spectrum-teach-36.
findings.verify_reason: bestRoute uses only [[]] (direct) for non-beam bands (logic.ts:187). legHits for TX→lab pad with radio gives only metal and glass at lab-front-a (x 4.50, z -3.2), and my logic-check output confirms it. Every radio and micro lab row, at all powers and both hatch states, is 'Metal shutter: Metal reflects radio: the shutter stops it.' LAB.door [9.4,11] has no wall (logic.ts:98), and 'lab-side' is brick (logic.ts:107). The hall draws broadcast rings (station.ts:392) and the map draws rings (station.ts:311). Extra evidence: the room builds the lab side wall as plain cream plaster (room.ts:77, toon('#efe6d8')), not the brick texture. The desk map strokes it brick-red (station.ts:292-293). So the player can't see in the hall that it is brick, but the map and logic say it is.
extra_evidence: src/stations/spectrum/room.ts:77 (lab side wall drawn as cream plaster, not brick)
findings.fix_correction: The opening-path pricing would make microwave through the open hatch a mirror-free job-2 solution. That is 10 dBm + 38 − ~21 spreading − 8 hatch − 2 glass ≈ 17 dB at 10 mW, which is reliable. NIR at 1 mW + mirror A stays the leanest, so Elegant is unchanged. But the job card, solver tests and logic.test.ts expectations need updating, and the designer should accept that alternate route on purpose. If lab-side becomes metal, also change room.ts:77 to the slat texture so the world matches the logic.

findings.title: The hole-versus-wavelength lesson (radio can't pass the hatch) can never happen, and the toast says 30 cm for a hatch that is 60 cm in the model and on screen
findings.problem: logic.ts:21-22 and :73 make the hatch a key guardrail: 'the 3 m radio wave cannot use a 30 cm hatch'. whyBlocked('hatch') holds the only explanation of aperture versus λ/2 (logic.ts:257). Radio and microwave never trace through the hatch: their direct ray TX(−0.4,2.3)→lab pad(7,−6) crosses lab-front-a at x≈4.5, which is metal. So the 'hatch' verdict and microwave's 8 dB hatch loss are unreachable. Every lab radio and microwave row in the sweep reads 'Metal shutter'. The size is also wrong: HATCH spans x 5.1–5.7 (0.6 m, logic.ts:87), the frame is 0.6 × 0.6 m (room.ts:87-90), and PROGRESS says 'The lab's hatch is 60 cm wide'. The toast still says 'a 30 cm hole' (station.ts:228). The c = f·λ number is printed on every band press (station.ts:222) but never drives a decision. In the world, the wavelength is never compared to a gap. The concept that explains both the hatch and the mesh is pure text.
findings.fix:
(1) Fix the number: change the toast at station.ts:228, the comment at logic.ts:22/73 and the message at logic.ts:257 to '60 cm'. Radio's λ/2 = 1.5 m is still far larger.
(2) Make the hatch reachable for broadcasts (see the opening-path fix in the lab finding), so a radio send with the hatch open fails on the 'hatch' message and microwave gets through it.
(3) Show λ to scale in the world. While radio or microwave is selected and Pip stands up, draw a wave ribbon from the tower at true wavelength: a 3 m arc for radio, small 12.5 cm ripples for microwave. Draw the λ/2 span as a bracket next to the hatch frame. The player can then see that the 1.5 m bracket doesn't fit the 0.6 m hatch, so the comparison becomes something seen in the world, not read.
findings.verify: Logic test: lab, radio, hatchOpen → judge().problems[0] contains 'Shutter hatch'. Retake spectrum-teach-15: the toast reads 60 cm. New hall shot with radio selected next to the hatch shows the λ/2 bracket.
findings.verify_reason: HATCH spans x 5.1 to 5.7, so 0.6 m (logic.ts:87). PROGRESS.md:297 and logic.test.ts:98 say 60 cm. The toast (station.ts:228), logic.ts:22, :73, :257 and logic.test.ts:23 still say 30 cm. Shot spectrum-teach-16 shows the '30 cm hole' toast in play. The hatch rule is unreachable: radio and micro always take the direct ray, which hits metal at x≈4.5. The only band with Infinity at 'hatch' is radio, which is never a beam. So whyBlocked('hatch') and micro's 8 dB hatch loss never come up (sweep: no 'Shutter hatch' verdict anywhere). I lowered the priority to P2. Hole-versus-λ isn't in the room's stated teaching list (docs/PROGRESS.md:168), so this is an untaught extra plus a wrong number (DR-34), not a false lesson in play.
findings.fix_correction: Also update the comment in logic.test.ts:23 to 60 cm.

findings.title: Sunlight in the 'sunny lab' can't be seen anywhere, so the reason near IR beats visible light can't be discovered
findings.problem:
Job 2's twist is ambient light: the visible photodiode loses 6 dB, the filtered NIR diode 2 dB (logic.ts:143-145, :151, :243). Nothing in the world or on the meters shows this:
- The lab interior looks like the hall, with no sun shafts or glare on the pad (shot 42).
- The link screen and panel show only the total margin, with no ambient term (station.ts:329-340, :423-427).
- The sunlight sentence appears only in tier-0 'Too weak' messages (logic.ts:271).

With visible light via mirror A at 1 mW the delivery is accepted as 'Received, but only 5.8 dB of margin' with no mention of the sun (shot 46, run3 log). The prompt then pushes 'P Power' (station.ts:443), and 10 mW gives 15.8 dB Reliable with 'uses more power than this delivery needs'. The player never learns that daylight is noise competing with the signal, or why a filtered near-IR detector fares better. The only way to find NIR is trial and error.
findings.fix:
(1) Room: in room.ts, add two soft sun shafts from the lab windows onto the pad (lampPool with a warm tint, opacity ≤ 0.35), plus a glare sprite on the pod's detector dome. Size the glare by the ambient term: big on the green photodiode, small on the near-IR dome.
(2) Meter: on the link screen (drawLink, station.ts:329), draw the ambient term as a grey 'sunlight' block with a sun icon eating into the bar from the left.
(3) Make the sun something to act on: R4B's lab blinds. A cord on the lab wall that Pip pulls (E) drops the blinds, sets job.ambient to 0, and lets visible light work at 1 mW. That is a second clean route and a physical act.
(4) Add an ambient note to tier 1/2 verdicts (logic.ts:273): 'Sunlight on the detector is eating 6 dB of margin.' This names the cause, not the fix.
findings.verify: Retake spectrum-teach-42 (sun shafts on the pad) and spectrum-teach-46 (the meter shows a sun block, the toast mentions sunlight). New logic test: blinds down gives vis 1 mW + mirror A reliable.
findings.verify_reason: In read(), ambient is applied only to vis (6 dB) and NIR (2 dB) (logic.ts:243). The sunlight text appears only in the tier-0 'Too weak' branch (logic.ts:271), and the tier-1 note has none (logic.ts:273). My logic check gives lab vis 1 mW + A = 5.8 dB 'Received, but only 5.8 dB of margin' with no sun mention. Shot spectrum-teach-46 shows exactly that toast. Vis at 10 mW gives 15.8 dB with 'more power than this delivery needs', so P (the suggested power key) gets a pass. Shot spectrum-teach-42 shows the lab with back windows (city view) but no light shafts or glare. The panel has no ambient row (station.ts:423-427).
extra_evidence: src/stations/spectrum/room.ts:59 (backWindows over the lab are the only sun cue)

findings.title: The link budget's terms are hidden: 'Path: clear' through 25 dB of smoke, one total in dB, and a 'P Power' prompt that pushes brute force
findings.problem: The model is a real link budget: P_tx + K − 20·log d − Σ obstacle losses − 1 dB per mirror − ambient (logic.ts:10-14). The player sees only the final number. The panel's 'Path' row says 'clear' whenever nothing has infinite loss (station.ts:426). Visible light through the tea-corner smoke reads 'Path: clear' at −12 dB (shots 22, 46), so the smoke, the cause, is invisible in the readout. 'dB margin is abstract' was already raised in R4B and is still true. Distance, mirrors, smoke and sun all collapse into one number, so the player can't tell which choice helped. When the margin is short the prompt is always 'P Power' (station.ts:443), which teaches 'turn it up' rather than 'remove the loss'.
findings.fix:
(1) Replace the link screen's single bar (station.ts:335-337) with a waterfall. Start at a 'sent' level (P_tx + K). Draw one coloured step down per term, each with its icon: distance (ruler), each obstacle crossed (brick, glass, mesh, smoke puff), each mirror, sunlight. End at the received level against the works and reliable lines. Draw it after SEND, from the pulse (see the commit-then-reveal finding).
(2) Change the panel's 'Path' row to list the crossings with their loss, e.g. 'smoke −25 · mesh −3'.
(3) Replace the 'P Power' prompt with 'Enter Send', or with nothing.
findings.verify: Retake spectrum-teach-23: the link screen shows a smoke step of about 25 dB, and the panel reads 'smoke −25'. Spec: with vis through the smoke, `.station-panel` contains 'smoke'.
findings.verify_reason: The Path row prints 'clear' whenever nothing has Infinity loss (station.ts:426). Shot spectrum-teach-23 shows 'Path clear' at −12.0 dB with 25 dB smoke and 3 dB mesh, plus the 'P Power' prompt (station.ts:443). In my own run, microwave through the storeroom brick (10 dB loss) also reads 'Path: clear, 7.0 dB'. The link screen draws one bar (station.ts:335-337). The 'P Power' prompt does lead to brute force: vis to the quiet room at 100 mW gives 8 dB and is delivered as tier 1 'Received' (logic-check). This also breaks DR-28: the cause, smoke, never appears in the readout.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-spectrum-teach/v1.mjs log: micro panel 'Path / clear / Link margin / 7.0 dB' through 10 dB of brick
logic-check: quiet vis 100 mW → tier 1, 8 dB

findings.title: A beam that misses the pod shows 'TOO WEAK' on the link screen, which points the player to power when the real problem is aim
findings.problem: When the aimed beam misses (route.missed), read() sets the margin to −Infinity (logic.ts:244). drawLink's status chain has no missed case, so it falls through to `m<SPEC.works` and prints 'TOO WEAK' in red (station.ts:338). Shot 13 shows the conflict: the panel says 'Path: misses the pod', the prompt says 'Aim, or another band', and the big link screen says TOO WEAK. The cause of a miss is geometry (angle in = angle out), but the biggest readout calls it a strength problem. The 1/10/100 mW keys sit right beside it, inviting a wrong fix that can never work.
findings.fix: In station.ts:338, insert `r.route.missed?['MISSES THE POD','#ffd66b']` before the TOO WEAK branch. Show 'missed' instead of 'no signal' for the value text at :334. Add `r.route.missed` to drawLink's redraw key at :330, which is already partly keyed on margin.
findings.verify: Retake spectrum-teach-13: the link screen reads MISSES THE POD. Add a station-spectrum spec assertion after `aim tx→A`, checking the link texture key or the panel text.
findings.verify_reason: Shot spectrum-teach-13 shows 'TOO WEAK' on the link screen while the panel says 'Path: misses the pod' and the prompt says 'Aim, or another band'. read() sets margin to −Infinity when missed (logic.ts:244), and the status chain has no missed branch (station.ts:338). It is real, but I lowered it to P2. The panel and the key prompt both name the real cause, and power can't make a missed send pass. It is a contradiction between readouts, not something that stops understanding.
findings.fix_correction: The redraw-key change isn't needed. A missed reading is already the only state with margin −Infinity, blocked=false, detectorOk=true and podOk=true, so the existing key (station.ts:330) already redraws it. Only the status branch and value text need to change.

findings.title: Messages, the job card and the wall chart give away the answers
findings.problem:
Several texts print the solution instead of the cause:
- The tier-0 smoke message ends 'long-wave thermal IR slips through' (logic.ts:271, shot 23). That is the job-3 answer, printed on the first visible-light failure.
- The mesh message ends 'Light passes between the wires' (logic.ts:258, shot 21), which narrows the choice to the optical bands.
- The job card step 4 reads 'Move the pod into the glass lab, and stand a mirror on a floor mark' (station.ts:89, shot 06). That names the tool for job 2 before the player has seen the shutter.
- The job-3 ask says 'Find a band that gets through both' (logic.ts:154).
- The 'WHAT GETS THROUGH?' chart on the hall wall (room.ts:134-140, shot 35) prints the full band × material answer matrix. Only one row (thermal) is green under both MESH and SMOKE, so job 3 can be read off the wall.

The player reads instead of doing. The 'aha' of reflecting a beam through the hatch is announced before the problem appears.
findings.fix:
(1) logic.ts:271: drop 'long-wave thermal IR slips through'. Keep 'Smoke scatters short wavelengths hardest.'
(2) logic.ts:258: end at '…so the mesh reflects it.'
(3) station.ts:89: 'Move the pod into the glass lab'. Make the mirror placement its own optional step that appears only after a send hits the shutter, or only mark the floor marks with the bouncing marker.
(4) logic.ts:154 ask: 'Burnt toast fills the tea corner with smoke, and the quiet room is a copper-mesh cage.' (drop the last sentence).
(5) Start the chart empty and fill each cell as it is observed (see the commit-then-reveal finding). At most, pre-fill only the glass column as a hint.
findings.verify: Grep logic.ts/station.ts for 'thermal IR slips', 'Light passes', 'stand a mirror'. All should be gone. Retake spectrum-teach-35 at start (an empty chart) and after job 1 (radio and visible cells filled for brick).
findings.verify_reason: I checked all the strings: logic.ts:271 ('long-wave thermal IR slips through', visible in shot 23), logic.ts:258 ('Light passes between the wires', shot 21), station.ts:89 (the job card names the mirror, also visible in shot 42's objective card), and logic.ts:154 ('Find a band that gets through both'). The chart matrix (room.ts:136) has thermal as the only row with 1 in both mesh and smoke, so job 3 can be read off the wall. The cited shot 35 does not show the chart; it shows the storeroom corner. My own close-up verify-spectrum-teach-01 does show the 'WHAT GETS THROUGH?' chart with its green/yellow/red dots readable on the side wall by the pod dock. This breaks DR-39 and DR-26.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/spectrum-teach-42-lab-interior-sunny.jpg (objective card 'Move the pod into the glass lab, and stand a mirror on a floor mark')

findings.title: Invisible bands are drawn in visible hues with no 'false colour' label: radio red, near IR hot pink, thermal orange
findings.problem: Each band has a display colour (logic.ts:48-52): radio #e5484d red, microwave orange, thermal IR amber, near IR #b0406a magenta, visible #3fae6a green. The beam in the hall uses that colour (station.ts:268-273), as do the tower beacon (:388), the map ray (:312), the band keys (:118) and the ribbon (:259). Shots 16 and 17 show a bright pink near-IR beam crossing the hall to the hatch. Shot 39 shows an orange thermal beam. Shot 37 shows red radio dashes. Real near IR and thermal IR are invisible, and radio isn't 'red'. The order (red, orange, amber, magenta, green) also isn't monotonic, which mixes 'red = long wave' with arbitrary hues. The only disclosure is 'ribbon not to scale' on the wave screen, and nothing says 'false colour'. This is the known DR-35 fail. It feeds the misconception that IR is a 'red-ish light' you can see, and that radio is a kind of light glowing red.
findings.fix:
Keep the real hue only for Visible.
(1) Draw invisible-band beams in the hall as a neutral white core with a band-specific pattern: dashes for radio, dots for microwave, a wavy shimmer for thermal, fine stripes for NIR. Or draw them through a 'detector view'.
(2) Add a mounted plaque on the tower and a line on the wave screen (station.ts:327): 'Invisible bands shown in false colour'.
(3) Map the false colours monotonically (one hue ramp from long to short wavelength) so the order itself teaches.
(4) Keep the band-key colours as UI tags, but give the four invisible keys a hatched cap.

findings.title: The 'Elegant' notes compare against a different band and so misattribute the waste ('more power than needed', 'more mirrors than it needs')
findings.problem:
judge() compares the player's setup with leanest(), the cheapest reliable setup over all bands (logic.ts:274-276, :292-295). Two misleading cases came up in play:
- (a) Storeroom with microwave at 10 mW: 10 mW is the minimum reliable power for microwave (1 mW gives 7 dB, sweep). The toast still says 'Reliable, but it uses more power than this delivery needs' (shot 41).
- (b) Quiet room with near IR routed around the smoke via mirror A at 1 mW, 11 dB: avoiding the scatter by going round it is a clever, truthful solution. It gets 'Reliable, but the beam bounces off more mirrors than it needs' (run3 log), because thermal needs 0 mirrors. For near IR that mirror is essential (without it 2 dB, sweep).

The player is told to cut power or mirrors, which would break their link. The real lesson, that a different band does better, stays hidden.
findings.fix:
In judge(), compute two references: `sameBand = solutions(job).filter(x=>x.setup.band===s.band)[0]` and `best = leanest(job)`.
- If sameBand uses less power or fewer mirrors: the current notes.
- Else if best uses less power or fewer mirrors: 'Reliable. Another band would get here with less.' This names no band, so it doesn't print the fix.

Add logic tests for both cases.
findings.verify: logic.test.ts: store, micro 10 mW → the note contains 'Another band'. Quiet, nir 1 mW + mirror A → the note does not contain 'mirrors than it needs'. Retake spectrum-teach-41.
findings.verify_reason: My logic check reproduces both cases. Store, micro 10 mW gives 17 dB with 'Reliable, but it uses more power than this delivery needs', though micro at 1 mW is only 7 dB, so 10 mW is micro's minimum. Quiet, NIR 1 mW + mirror A gives 11 dB with 'Reliable, but the beam bounces off more mirrors than it needs', though NIR without the mirror is 2 dB. The cause is judge() comparing against leanest() across all bands (logic.ts:274-276, :292-295).
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-spectrum-teach/logic-check.ts output: 'store micro 10 … uses more power', 'quiet nir via A … more mirrors than it needs', 'quiet nir 1 (no mirror) tier 1, 2 dB'

findings.title: Matching the detector to the band can never come up in play: the pod fits the matching head by itself
findings.problem: PROGRESS lists 'detector matching' as one of this room's ideas (docs/PROGRESS.md:168), and logic.ts:23 makes it a guardrail ('A detector only responds to its own band'). act('band') sets `this.detector=BANDS[b].detector` (station.ts:221), so the player never chooses a detector. The 'WRONG DETECTOR' status (station.ts:338) and the wrong-detector problem text (logic.ts:266-267) are dead in normal play. R4B called the separate menu redundant, and that is fixed. But the fix deleted the idea instead of making it physical. The R4B redesign ('Detector heads are props snapped onto the pod') was not built. That a dipole antenna, a thermopile and a photodiode are physically different sensors for different wavelengths is a strong, truthful idea, and it is now gone.
findings.fix:
Make the head a carried prop.
(1) Place the five headMesh models (station.ts:46-53) on a rack by the pod dock as id'd grabbables.
(2) Pip carries the right head to the pod at its pad and snaps it on with F, which reuses the plug snap.
(3) The pod's lamp stays red with a sad static sound when the band and head don't match.
(4) Drop the automatic assignment at station.ts:221.

This also adds the walk-and-fetch physical act that DR-05 asks for in a cable-less room. Keep it forgiving: the pod accepts any head, and the mismatch shows as the WRONG DETECTOR status with no send needed.
findings.verify: Spec: radio with the green photodiode head fails with 'only responds to'. After swapping to the dipole it passes. Shot of the pod with each head.
findings.verify_reason: act('band') always sets detector = BANDS[b].detector (station.ts:221), and nothing else in the station changes this.detector. That makes the WRONG DETECTOR branch (station.ts:338) and the problem text (logic.ts:266-267) dead code in play, while PROGRESS.md:168 lists 'detector matching' as taught. The R4B redesign (heads as props) wasn't built (mockups/review4/DESIGN_B.md 'Detector heads are props snapped onto the pod'). P2 is right: removing the redundant menu was a deliberate choice, and the room still teaches its other ideas.
extra_evidence: mockups/review4/DESIGN_B.md (Spectrum redesign: 'Detector heads are props snapped onto the pod')
findings.fix_correction: Drop the DR-05 justification. DR-05 asks for a cable act (drag, route, wrap, plug, slingshot). Carrying a detector head is a prop act, not a cable act, so it doesn't meet DR-05. Also, 'the mismatch shows as the WRONG DETECTOR status with no send needed' is the live preview that finding 0 wants removed. Show the mismatch on the pod itself instead (red lamp and static, DR-47), and leave the desk readout until after SEND.

findings.title: The thermal IR link has no background, though everything at room temperature (and the hot toaster sitting in the beam) glows at 10 µm
findings.problem: read() applies ambient only to visible and near IR (logic.ts:243). By Wien's law, objects at about 300 K radiate most strongly near 10 µm, so walls, coworkers and especially the hot toaster in the tea corner (room.ts:112) are bright thermal-IR sources right where the beam passes. Job 3's winning band, thermal IR at 1 mW, gets a clean 15 dB with zero background. Thermal through smoke is true and well anchored (firefighting thermal cameras, scattering negligible at 8–14 µm), and glass being opaque at 10 µm is also correct. But the clean link teaches that thermal IR is a quiet channel. In fact it is the noisiest, which is why it is used for imaging heat, not for messaging. At this level it can stay simplified. It needs an acknowledgement, or a small cost.
findings.fix: Give thermal a small ambient term: 3 dB near the toaster, i.e. when the leg passes within SMOKE.r (logic.ts:243). Thermal at 1 mW then gives 12 dB, still reliable and still leanest. Add a tier note: 'Warm things glow in thermal IR too; the toaster adds background.' The example line (logic.ts:50) could read 'heat cameras (see through smoke)' to anchor the true use.
findings.verify: Logic test: quiet, thermal 1 mW → margin 12 dB and tier 3. Retake spectrum-teach-24.
findings.verify_reason: The key factual premise is wrong. The toaster isn't 'in the beam'. It sits at about (2.1, 4.85) (tea group 2.4,4.85 with toaster at −0.3; room.ts:111-112). The thermal ray TX→quiet pad passes at z≈3.03 at that x, about 1.8 m away, just clipping the smoke cloud edge (closest approach 0.27 m from SMOKE centre). The physics claim is also overstated. Long-wave IR free-space links are a real research and engineering use, chosen precisely because 8 to 14 µm passes smoke and fog. Room-temperature background is a mostly constant (DC) level that a modulated link rejects, so leaving it out is a fair simplification at the level taught, not a falsehood under AGENTS 10. The game never claims thermal IR is a 'quiet channel'. At most the optional anchor line 'heat cameras (see through smoke)' is a harmless nicety.
extra_evidence: Geometry: TX(-0.4,2.3)→quiet(8.2,4.8) at x=2.1 gives z≈3.03, about 1.8 m from the toaster
findings.fix_correction: Don't add a toaster ambient term. If anything, change the example string at logic.ts:50 to 'heat cameras (see through smoke)' as a P2 anchor.

findings.title: The win push-in frames the tower and desk, not the pod receiving the message through the cage
findings.problem: On the last delivery the camera pushes in on the desk and the tower (shots 25 and 48). The pulse arrival and the star burst at the quiet-room pad (station.ts:235, :396) are off-frame. So is the pod's green lamp. Pip faces the camera with the transmitter behind. The payoff of the lesson, the thermal beam crossing smoke and mesh and landing, isn't shown. During deliveries at the desk, the hall beam and pulse are hidden (station.ts:374, :390, :397). The only success feedback is the map, the toast and confetti over the desk.
findings.fix: On each successful SEND, leave the bench camera for about 1.5 s on a fly-along. Have the camera follow the pulse along drawnPath at about 9 m/s, show the stop or arrival burst at the pad with the pod lamp turning green and the recipient blob cheering, then return. For the final win, set the station's winFocus to the last pad plus Pip, or have the game's win focus use `PADS[lastJob.pad]`.
findings.verify: Win screenshot: the quiet-room pad, the pod lamp and the arriving beam are inside the centre 70 % of the frame.
findings.verify_reason: Shot spectrum-teach-25 frames Pip, the desk screens and the tower, but not the quiet-room pad or the pod. winFocus with a station returns station.table (src/game.ts:398). At the desk, the hall pulse is hidden (station.ts:397), and the pad star burst only fires when !atBench (station.ts:235), so the arrival is never on screen. One correction: DR-11's letter (Pip plus the working machine in frame) is arguably met, because the desk and tower are the machine. This is lost payoff (fun), not a rule break.
findings.fix_correction: Keep any automatic fly-along short (≤ 1.5 s) and cancel it on any camera input, so it respects the player-controlled orbit camera rule. A simpler first step is to let the Station give its own winFocus: the midpoint of the last pad and the desk, with distance enough to frame both.

notes.teaching:
Electronics truth, strengths: the physics in logic.ts is mostly sound and well commented. The ideas checked out: c = f·λ for all bands; one 20·log d spreading law for every band (the R4B 10·log d bug is fixed); brick passing radio but stopping light; window glass opaque to 10 µm thermal IR (confirmed: thermal cameras can't see through windows); smoke scattering short wavelengths hardest, with LWIR passing (confirmed: scattering is negligible at 8–14 µm, which is why firefighters use thermal cameras); metal reflecting everything; a mesh passing light but not RF; and a hole much smaller than λ/2 blocking a wave.

Where teaching falls short: the room doesn't make the concept the mechanic. The wavelength-versus-material decision is a 5-key list. The result (CLEAR LINK, margin in dB, Path clear or blocked) shows live before committing, so trying each band in turn solves every job at no cost. Prompts ('another band', 'P Power') and messages ('long-wave thermal IR slips through', 'Light passes between the wires') print the answers. The wall chart is the full answer key. The reason behind the mesh and the hatch, the ratio of wavelength to gap size, is never something the player sees or uses:
- the hatch verdict can't be reached;
- the toast says 30 cm while the hatch is 60 cm;
- the mesh drawn on screen has holes at λ/2 of Wi-Fi.

Several simplifications would mislead a careful learner: the 'Faraday cage' has an open doorway and only two mesh sides; the lab blocks radio 'by the shutter' although its side wall is brick and its door is open, which contradicts job 1. Broadcast bands are drawn as rings but scored as one straight ray. Sunlight, the key to job 2, is invisible. Invisible bands are drawn in vivid false colours with no label.

The moment where the player really applies an idea is aiming mirrors (angle in = angle out) through the hatch, and that part works.
notes.fun:
Carrying the pod and standing mirror boards on the floor marks gives the room a physical, Good Job-style shape. The hand-aimed hall map with the live ray bouncing off the board (shots 13-15) is the best toy in the room: the beam flips back off an idle mirror, then swings through the hatch. The deliveries are short (about 50 s for a clean run), and the three obstacles are distinct.

What's missing:
- Success happens off-screen: the beam and the pulse are hidden while Pip sits at the desk, and the win shot frames the tower, not the pod.
- No chaos or alternate physical route exists: no blinds to pull, no cage door to prop open, no detector heads to swap, no coworkers walking through the beam.

Each of those would be a funny physical act that also teaches.
notes.playability: The full clean route completed with zero console errors in run1 and run3. Failed sends are explained and recoverable at once with another band or another aim (DR-20 passes). The prompts track the desk state, but they steer toward brute force: 'P Power' whenever the margin is short, and 'Another band' whenever the path is blocked. A missed aim reads 'TOO WEAK' on the big link screen, so the wrong fix (more power) looks plausible. Walking the pod between rooms three times is the main time cost. It is fine at about 15 s per leg.
notes.clarity:
Bench layout:
- Band keys on the left with the wave ribbon; the live hall map in the centre; power, hatch and SEND on the right.
- The two screens show λ, f and the link meter. The panel repeats band, power, path and margin.
- That puts the same value in two places (DR-41): band and λ on the wave screen and the panel; margin on the link screen and the panel.

Text problems:
- The disclosure lines ('ribbon not to scale', 'works'/'reliable') are about 5 px tall.
- The link screen's status ignores a missed beam.
- 'Path: clear' is shown even through 25 dB of smoke.
- The job card names the method ('stand a mirror on a floor mark').
- The floor marks and pads read well at the game camera. The HATCH and GLASS LAB signs are mounted, and the hatch frame is clearly yellow.
notes.models: Not this reviewer's dimension. Noted only where a model carries the lesson: the copper mesh texture's 6.25 cm cells contradict 'holes far smaller than the wavelength', and the 0.6 m hatch frame contradicts the 30 cm toast. The lab has no visible sunlight. The pod's detector heads are modelled distinctly (dipole, patch, horn, domes) but swap automatically, so their shapes teach nothing.
